Cahn-Hilliard Equations and Phase Transition Dynamics for Binary SystemsThanks: The work was supported in part by the Office of Naval Research and by the National Science Foundation.

Tian Ma TMDepartment of Mathematics, Sichuan University, Chengdu, P. R. China and Shouhong Wang SWDepartment of Mathematics, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN 47405 Email address: showang@indiana.edu
Abstract.

The process of phase separation of binary systems is described by the Cahn-Hilliard equation. The main objective of this article is to give a classification on the dynamic phase transitions for binary systems using either the classical Cahn-Hilliard equation or the Cahn-Hilliard equation coupled with entropy, leading to some interesting physical predictions. The analysis is based on dynamic transition theory for nonlinear systems and new classification scheme for dynamic transitions, developed recently by the authors.

1. Introduction

Cahn-Hilliard equation describes the process of phase separation, by which the two components of a binary fluid spontaneously separate and form domains pure in each component. The main objective of this article is to provide a theoretical approach to dynamic phase transitions for binary systems.

Classically, phase transitions are classified by the Ehrenfest classification scheme, based on the lowest derivative of the free energy that is discontinuous at the transition. In general, it is a difficult task to classify phase transitions of higher order, which appears in many equilibrium phase transition systems, such as the PVT system, the ferromagnetic system, superfluids as well as the binary systems studied in this article.

For this purpose, a new dynamic transition theory is developed recently by the authors. This new theory provides an efficient tool to analyze phase transitions of higher order. With this theory in our disposal, a new dynamic classification scheme is obtained, and classifies phase transitions into three categories: Type-I, Type-II and Type-III, corresponding mathematically to continuous, jump, and mixed transitions, respectively; see the Appendix as well as two recent books by the authors [3, 4] for details.

There have been extensive studies in the past on the dynamics of the Cahn-Hilliard equations. However, very little is known about the higher order transitions encountered for this problem, and this article gives a complete classification of the dynamics transitions for binary systems. The results obtained lead in particular to various physical predictions. First, the order of phase transitions is precisely determined by the sign of a nondimensional parameter KK such that if K>0K>0, the transition is first-order with latent heat and if K<0K<0, the transition is second-order. Second, a theoretical transition diagram is derived, leading in particular to a prediction that there is only second-order transition for molar fraction near 1/21/2. This is different from the prediction made by the classical transition diagram. Third, a critical length scale is derived such that no phase separation occurs at any temperature if the length of the container is smaller than the critical length scale. These physical predictions will be addressed in another article.

This article is organized as follows. In Section 2, both the classical Cahn-Hilliard equation and the Cahn-Hilliard equation coupled with entropy are introduced in a unified fashion using a general principle for equilibrium phase transitions outlined in Appendix B. Sections 3-6 analyze dynamic transitions for the Cahn-Hilliard equation in general domain, rectangular domain, with periodic boundary conditions, and for the Cahn-Hilliard equation coupled with entropy. Physical conclusions are given in Section 7, and the dynamic transition theory is recalled in Appendix A.

2. Dynamic Phase Transition Models for Binary Systems

Materials compounded by two components AA and BB, such as binary alloys, binary solutions and polymers, are called binary systems. Sufficient cooling of a binary system may lead to phase separations, i.e., at the critical temperature, the concentrations of both components AA and BB with homogeneous distribution undergo changes, leading to heterogeneous distributions in space. Phase separation of binary systems observed will be in one of two main ways. The first is by nucleation in which sufficiently large nuclei of the second phase appear randomly and grow, and this corresponds to Type-II phase transitions. The second is by spinodal decomposition in which the systems appear to nuclear at once, and periodic or semi-periodic structure is seen, and this corresponds to Type-I phase transitions.

Since binary systems are conserved, the equations describing the Helmholtz process and the Gibbs process are the same. Hence, without distinction we use the term ”free energy” to discuss this problem.

Let uAu_{A} and uBu_{B} be the concentrations of components AA and BB respectively, then uB=1−uAu_{B}=1-u_{A}. In a homogeneous state, uB=u¯Bu_{B}=\bar{u}_{B} is a constant, and the entropy density S0=S¯0S_{0}=\bar{S}_{0} is also a constant. We take u,Su,S the concentration and entropy density deviations:

u=uB−u¯B,S=S0−S¯0u=u_{B}-\bar{u}_{B},\ \ \ \ S=S_{0}-\bar{S}_{0}

Let γ2≠0\gamma_{2}\neq 0, γ3>0\gamma_{3}>0, and x=0x=0 be an isolated singular point of (3.13). Then the phase transition of (3.1) and (3.5) is either Type-II or Type-III. Remark 3.1.

We shall see later that when Ω\Omega is a rectangular domain, i.e.,

Ω=Πk=1n​(0,Lk)⊂ℝn(1≤n≤3),\Omega=\Pi^{n}_{k=1}(0,L_{k})\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}\qquad(1\leq n\leq 3),

then a=∫Ωe13​𝑑x=0a=\int_{\Omega}e_{1}^{3}dx=0. However, for almost all non-rectangular domains Ω\Omega, the first eigenvalues are simple and a≠0a\neq 0. Hence, the Type-III phase transitions for general domains are generic.∎

Proof of Theorem 3.2.

Assertions (1)-(3) can be directly proved using Theorems A.5, A.8, and A.9. By assumption, u=0u=0 is a second order non-degenerate singular point of (3.3) at λ=ρ1\lambda=\rho_{1}, which implies that u=0u=0 is not locally asymptotically stable. Hence, it follows from Theorems A.3 and the steady state bifurcation theorem for even-order nondegenerate singular points [3] that the phase transition of (3.1) with (3.5) is either Type-II or Type-III, and there is at least one singular point bifurcated on each side of λ=ρ1\lambda=\rho_{1}.

Finally, we shall apply Theorem A.6 to prove that there exists a saddle-node bifurcation on λ<ρ1\lambda<\rho_{1}.

It is known that

ind(Lλ+G,0)={even if ​λ=ρ1,1 if ​λ<ρ1.\text{ind}(L_{\lambda}+G,0)=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\text{even}&&\text{ if }\lambda=\rho_{1},\\ &1&&\text{ if }\lambda<\rho_{1}.\end{aligned}\right.

Moreover, since Lλ+GL_{\lambda}+G defined by (3.2) is a gradient-type operator, we can derive that

ind​(Lρ1+G,0)≤0.\text{ind}(L_{\rho_{1}}+G,0)\leq 0.

Hence there is a bifurcated branch Σλ\Sigma_{\lambda} on λ<ρ1\lambda<\rho_{1} such that

ind​(Lλ+G,uλ)=−1∀uλ∈Σλ,λ<ρ1.\text{ind}(L_{\lambda}+G,u_{\lambda})=-1\qquad\forall u_{\lambda}\in\Sigma_{\lambda},\ \ \ \ \lambda<\rho_{1}.

It is clear that the eigenvalues (3.6) of LλL_{\lambda} satisfy (A.4) and (A.5). For any λ∈ℝ1\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{1} (3.3) possesses a global attractor. Therefore, for bounded λ,b<λ≤ρ1\lambda,b<\lambda\leq\rho_{1}, the bifurcated branch Σλ\Sigma_{\lambda} is bounded:

‖uλ‖H≤C∀uλ∈Σλ,−∞<b<λ≤ρ1.\|u_{\lambda}\|_{H}\leq C\qquad\forall u_{\lambda}\in\Sigma_{\lambda},\ \ \ \ -\infty<b<\lambda\leq\rho_{1}.

We need to prove that there exists λ~<ρ1\widetilde{\lambda}<\rho_{1} such that for all λ<λ~\lambda<\widetilde{\lambda} equation (3.3) has no nonzero singular points.

By the energy estimates of (3.3), for any λ<λ~=−γ22/2γ3\lambda<\widetilde{\lambda}=-{\gamma^{2}_{2}}/{2\gamma_{3}} and u≠0u\neq 0 in HH,

∫Ω[|Δ​u|2−λ​|∇u|2+2​γ2​u​|∇u|2+3​γ3​u2​|∇u|2]​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\left[|\Delta u|^{2}-\lambda|\nabla u|^{2}+2\gamma_{2}u|\nabla u|^{2}+3\gamma_{3}u^{2}|\nabla u|^{2}\right]dx
≥∫Ω|Δ​u|2​𝑑x+∫Ω|∇u|2​(−λ−2​|γ2​u|+3​γ3​u2)​𝑑x\displaystyle\geq\int_{\Omega}|\Delta u|^{2}dx+\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}(-\lambda-2|\gamma_{2}u|+3\gamma_{3}u^{2})dx
≥∫Ω|∇u|2​𝑑x+∫Ω|∇u|2​(−λ+γ3​u2+2​γ3​(u−γ2γ3)2−γ222​γ3)​𝑑x\displaystyle\geq\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}dx+\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}(-\lambda+\gamma_{3}u^{2}+2\gamma_{3}(u-\frac{\gamma_{2}}{\gamma_{3}})^{2}-\frac{\gamma^{2}_{2}}{2\gamma_{3}})dx
≥∫Ω|∇u|2​𝑑x+∫Ω|∇u|2​(−λ−γ222​γ3)​𝑑x\displaystyle\geq\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}dx+\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}(-\lambda-\frac{\gamma^{2}_{2}}{2\gamma_{3}})dx
>0.\displaystyle>0.

Therefore, when λ<λ~\lambda<\widetilde{\lambda}, (3.3) has no nontrivial singular points in HH. Thus we infer from Theorem A.6 that there exists a saddle-node bifurcation on λ<ρ1\lambda<\rho_{1}. This proof is complete. ∎

4. Phase Transition in Rectangular Domains

The dynamical properties of phase separation of a binary system in a rectangular container is very different from that in a general container. We see in the previous section that the phase transitions in general domains are Type-III, and we shall show in the following that the phase transitions in rectangular domains are either Type-I or Type-II, which are distinguished by a critical size of the domains.

Remark 4.2.

In Theorem 4.2, the minimal attractors in the bifurcated attractor Σλ\Sigma_{\lambda} can be expressed as

(4.34) uλ=(λ−π2/L2)1/2​e+o⁡(|λ−π2/L2|1/2),u_{\lambda}=(\lambda-\pi^{2}/L^{2})^{{1}/{2}}e+o(|\lambda-\pi^{2}/L^{2}|^{{1}/{2}}),

where ee is a first eigenfunction of (3.4). The expression (4.34) can be derived from the reduced equations (4.18).

We address here that the exponent β=1/2\beta={1}/{2} in (4.34), called the critical exponent in physics, is an important index in the phase transition theory in statistical physics, which arises only in the Type-I or the continuous phase transitions. It is interesting to point out that the critical exponent β=1\beta=1 in (3.14) is different from these β=1/2\beta={1}/{2} appearing in (4.2) and (4.34). The first one occurs when the container Ω⊂ℝ3\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{3} is a non rectangular region, and the second one occurs when Ω\Omega is a rectangle or a cube. We shall continue to discuss this problem later from the physical viewpoint. ∎

5. Phase Transitions Under Periodic Boundary Conditions

When the sample or container Ω\Omega is a loop, or a torus, or bulk in size, then the periodic boundary conditions are necessary. In this section, we shall discuss the problems in a loop domain and in the whole space Ω=ℝn\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{n}.

Let Ω=S1×(r1,r2)⊂ℝ2\Omega=S^{1}\times(r_{1},r_{2})\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be a loop domain, 0<r1<r20<r_{1}<r_{2}. Then the boundary condition is given by

7. Physical remarks

We now address the physical significance for the phase transition theorems obtained in the previous sections.

7.1. Equation of critical parameters

For a binary system, the equation describing the control parameters T,p,ΩT,p,\Omega at the critical states is simple.

We first consider the critical temperature TcT_{c}. There are two different critical temperatures T1T_{1} and T0T_{0} in the Cahn-Hilliard equation. T1T_{1} is the one given by (2.8), at which the coefficient b1​(T,p)b_{1}(T,p) or λ=−l2b1(T,p)/k\lambda=-l^{2}b_{1}(T,p)/k will change its sign, and T0T_{0} satisfies that λ0<λ1\lambda_{0}<\lambda_{1}, and for fixed pp,

(7.1) λ(T){<ρ1 if ​T>T0,=ρ1 if ​T=T0,>ρ1 if ​T<T0,\lambda(T)\left\{\begin{aligned} &<\rho_{1}&&\text{ if }T>T_{0},\\ &=\rho_{1}&&\text{ if }T=T_{0},\\ &>\rho_{1}&&\text{ if }T<T_{0},\end{aligned}\right.

Equation (7.6) gives the critical parameter curve of a binary system with constant pressure for temperature TT and diameter scaling LL of container Ω\Omega. Because T≥0T\geq 0, from (7.5) we can deduce the following physical conclusion.

Physical Conclusion 7.1. Under constant pressure, for any binary system with given geometrical shape of the container Ω\Omega, there is a value L0>0L_{0}>0 such that as the diameter scaling L<L0L<L_{0}, no phase separation takes place at all temperature T≥0T\geq 0, and as L>L0L>L_{0} phase separation will occur at some critical temperature T0>0T_{0}>0 satisfying (7.6).

We shall see later that it is a universal property that the dynamical properties of phase transitions depend on the geometrical shape and size of the container or sample Ω\Omega.

7.2. Physical explanations of phase transition theorems

We first briefly recall the classical thermodynamic theory for a binary system. Physically, phase separation processes taking place in an unstable state are called spinodal decompositions; see Cahn and Hilliard [1] and Onuki [6]. When consider the concentration uu as homogeneous in Ω\Omega, then by (7.5) the dynamic equation of a binary system is an ordinary differential equation:

(7.7) d​ud​t=−d​gd​u=2​a​u−R​T​ln⁡u1−u+μA−μB−a.\frac{du}{dt}=-\frac{dg}{du}=2au-RT\ln\frac{u}{1-u}+\mu_{A}-\mu_{B}-a.

where

It is clear that the critical parameter curve λ=0\lambda=0 in the T−u0T-u_{0} plane is given by

T0=2​a​u0​(1−u0)/R,T_{0}=2au_{0}(1-u_{0})/R,

which is schematically illustrated in the classical phase diagram; see the dotted line in Figure 7.1. We obtain from (7.8) the following transition steady states:

v±=−12​b3​(b2±b22−4​b3​λ) for ​b22−4​b3​λ>0.v^{\pm}=\frac{-1}{2b_{3}}(b_{2}\pm\sqrt{b_{2}^{2}-4b_{3}\lambda})\qquad\text{ for }b_{2}^{2}-4b_{3}\lambda>0.

such that if T0<T<T∗T_{0}<T<T^{*},

Here

is illustrated by the solid line in Figure 7.1. This shows that the region T0​(u0)<T<T∗​(u0)T_{0}(u_{0})<T<T^{*}(u_{0}) is metastable, which is marked by the shadowed region in Figure 7.1. See, among others, Reichl [7], Novick-Cohen and Segal [5] , and Langer [2] for the phase transition diagram from the classical thermodynamic theory.

In the following we shall discuss the spinodal decomposition in a unified fashion by applying the phase transition theorems presented in the previous sections.

As mentioned in the Introduction, phase separation processes of binary systems occur in two ways, one of which proceeds continuously depending on TT, and the other one does not. Obviously, the classical theory does not explain these phenomena. In fact, the first one can be described by the Type-I phase transition, and the second one can be explained by the Type-II and Type-III phase transitions.

We first consider the case where the container Ω=Πi=1n​(0,Li)\Omega=\Pi^{n}_{i=1}(0,L_{i}) with L=L1=⋯=Lm>Lj​(j>m)L=L_{1}=\cdots=L_{m}>L_{j}(j>m) is a rectangular domain. Thus, by Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 (or Theorem 6.1) there are only two phase transition types: Type-I and Type-II, with the type of transition depending on LL. We see that if

L2<{92​π2​γ3γ22for​m=1,2726​π2​γ3γ22for​m≥2,L^{2}<\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{9}{2}\frac{\pi^{2}\gamma_{3}}{\gamma^{2}_{2}}&&\text{for}\ m=1,\\ &\frac{27}{26}\frac{\pi^{2}\gamma_{3}}{\gamma^{2}_{2}}&&\text{for}\ m\geq 2,\end{aligned}\right.

then the transition is Type-I, i.e., the phase pattern formation gradually varies as the temperature decreases. In this case, no meta-stable states and no latent heat appear. The phase diagram is given by Figure 7.2, where the solid lines uiTu_{i}^{T} (i=1,2i=1,2) represent the transition solutions.

If LL satisfies that

L2>{92​π2​γ3γ22for​m=1,2726​π2​γ3γ22for​m≥2,L^{2}>\left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{9}{2}\frac{\pi^{2}\gamma_{3}}{\gamma^{2}_{2}}&&\text{for}\ m=1,\\ &\frac{27}{26}\frac{\pi^{2}\gamma_{3}}{\gamma^{2}_{2}}&&\text{for}\ m\geq 2,\end{aligned}\right.

then the phase transition is Type-II. Namely, there is a leaping change in phase pattern formation at the critical temperature TcT_{c}. The phase diagram for Type-II transition is given by Figure 7.3.

In Figure 7.3, T0T_{0} is the critical temperature as in (7.1), T∗T^{*} is defined by (7.9) and is the saddle-node bifurcation point of (7.8). The constant concentration u=u0u=u_{0} is stable in Tc<TT_{c}<T, is meta-stable in T0<T<TcT_{0}<T<T_{c}, and is unstable in T<T0T<T_{0}. The two bifurcated states U1TU^{T}_{1} and U2TU^{T}_{2} from T∗T^{*} are meta-stable in T0<T<T∗T_{0}<T<T^{*}, and are stable in T<T0T<T_{0}. Here for i=1,2i=1,2, UiT=uiT+u0U_{i}^{T}=u^{T}_{i}+u_{0}, and uiu_{i} are the separated solutions of (3.1) with (3.5) from T∗T^{*}.

There is a remarkable difference between Type-I and Type-II transitions. The Type-I phase transition occurs at T=T0T=T_{0} and Type-II does in T0<T<T∗T_{0}<T<T^{*}. Furthermore, latent heat is accompanied the Type-II phase transition. Actually, when a binary system undergoes a transition from u0u_{0} to UiTU^{T}_{i} (i=1,2)(i=1,2), there is a gap |UiT−u0|2=|uiT|2>ε>0|U^{T}_{i}-u_{0}|^{2}=|u_{i}^{T}|^{2}>\varepsilon>0 for any T0<T<T∗T_{0}<T<T^{*}. By the first equation in (6.1) it yields a jump of entropy between u0u_{0} and UiTU^{T}_{i}:

δSi=∫ΩSdx=−α2α1∫Ω|uTi|2dx<0,\delta S_{i}=\int_{\Omega}Sdx=-\frac{\alpha_{2}}{\alpha_{1}}\int_{\Omega}|u^{T}_{i}|^{2}dx<0,

where S=Si−S¯0S=S_{i}-\bar{S}_{0} represents the entropy density deviation. Hence the latent heat is given by

δH=TδSi=−α2​Tα1∫Ω|uTi|2dx<0,\delta H=T\delta S_{i}=-\frac{\alpha_{2}T}{\alpha_{1}}\int_{\Omega}|u^{T}_{i}|^{2}dx<0,

which implies that the process from u0u_{0} to UiTU^{T}_{i} is exothermic, and the process from UiTU^{T}_{i} to u0u_{0} is endothermic.

Now, we consider the case where the container Ω\Omega is non rectangular. Thus, by Theorem 3.2 the transition is Type-III, and its phase diagram is given by Figure 7.4.

In Figure 7.4, T0T_{0} and T∗T^{*} are the same as those in Figure 7.3. The state u0u_{0} is stable in T∗<TT^{*}<T, is metastable in T0<T<T∗T_{0}<T<T^{*}, and unstable in T<T0T<T_{0}. The equilibrium state U1TU^{T}_{1} separated from T∗T^{*} is metastable in T0<T<T∗T_{0}<T<T^{*}, and is stable in T<T0T<T_{0}. However, the equilibrium state U2TU^{T}_{2} separated from T∗T^{*} is unstable in T0<T<T∗T_{0}<T<T^{*}, and is metastable in T<T0T<T_{0}.

Similar to the Type-II, the Type-III phase transition has also latent heat, which occurs in T0<T<T∗T_{0}<T<T^{*}. But the difference between Type-II and Type-III is that Type-II has 2​m2m (m≥1)(m\geq 1) stable equilibrium states separated from T=T∗T=T^{*}, but Type-III has just one. The 2​m2m stable states of a Type-II transition are of some symmetry caused by Ω\Omega, and we shall investigate it later. A particular aspect of Type-III is that there is a state U2TU^{T}_{2} bifurcated from (u,T)=(u0,T0)(u,T)=(u_{0},T_{0}), which is rarely observed in experiments.

7.3. Symmetry and periodic structure

Physical experiments have shown that in pattern formation via phase separation, periodic or semi-periodic structure appears. From Theorems 5.1 and 5.2 we see that for the loop domains and bulk domains which can be considered as ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} or ℝm×D\mathbb{R}^{m}\times D (D⊂ℝn−m)(D\subset\mathbb{R}^{n-m}) the steady state solutions of the Cahn-Hilliard equation are periodic, and for rectangular domains they are semi-periodic, and the periodicity is associated with the mirror image symmetry.

Let Ω=(0,L)m×D\Omega=(0,L)^{m}\times D (m≥1)(m\geq 1). By Remark 4.1, Theorem 4.1 is valid for Ω\Omega. Actually, in this case the following space

H~={u∈L2(Ω)|u=∑|K|=1∞ykcosk1​πLx1⋯coskm​πLxm}⊂H\widetilde{H}=\left\{u\in L^{2}(\Omega)|\ u=\sum^{\infty}_{|K|=1}y_{k}\cos\frac{k_{1}\pi}{L}x_{1}\cdots\cos\frac{k_{m}\pi}{L}x_{m}\right\}\subset H

is invariant for the Cahn-Hilliard equation (3.1) and (3.5). All separated equilibrium states in Theorem 4.1 are in H~\widetilde{H}. From the physical viewpoint, all equilibrium states u⁡(x)u(x) and their mirror image states u⁡(L−x′,x′′)u(L-x^{\prime},x^{\prime\prime}) are the same to describe the pattern formation. Mathematically, under the mirror image transformation

x→(L−x′,x′′),x′=(x1,⋯,xm),x′′=(xm+1,⋯,xn),x\rightarrow(L-x^{\prime},x^{\prime\prime}),\ \ \ \ x^{\prime}=(x_{1},\cdots,x_{m}),\ \ \ \ x^{\prime\prime}=(x_{m+1},\cdots,x_{n}),

7.4. Critical exponents

From (4.2) and (4.34) we see that for Type-I phase transition of a binary system the critical exponent β=12\beta=\frac{1}{2}. In this case, it is a second order phase transition with the Ehrenfest classification scheme, and there is a gap in heat capacity at critical temperature T0T_{0}. To see this, by (4.2) and (4.34) we have

uT={0if​T0<T,α​(λ⁡(T)−π2/L2)1/2​e1+o⁡(|λ−π2/L2|1/2)if​T<T0,u^{T}=\left\{\begin{aligned} &0&&\text{if}\ T_{0}<T,\\ &\alpha(\lambda(T)-\pi^{2}/L^{2})^{{1}/{2}}e_{1}+o(|\lambda-\pi^{2}/L^{2}|^{{1}/{2}})&&\text{if}\ T<T_{0},\end{aligned}\right.

and the free energy for (3.1) at uTu^{T} is

F⁡(uT)=\displaystyle F(u^{T})= ∫Ω[12​|∇uT|2−λ2​|uT|2+o⁡(|uT|2)]​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\left[\frac{1}{2}|\nabla u^{T}|^{2}-\frac{\lambda}{2}|u^{T}|^{2}+o(|u^{T}|^{2})\right]dx
=\displaystyle= ∫Ω12​[−Δ​uT−λ​uT]​uT+13​γ2​(uT)3+14​γ3​(uT)4​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\frac{1}{2}[-\Delta u^{T}-\lambda u^{T}]u^{T}+\frac{1}{3}\gamma_{2}(u^{T})^{3}+\frac{1}{4}\gamma_{3}(u^{T})^{4}dx
=\displaystyle= {0if​T0<T,−α22(λ−π2/L2)2⋅∫Ω[e21+α24γ3e41]dx+o(|λ−π2/L2|2)if​T>T0.\displaystyle\left\{\begin{aligned} &0&&\text{if}\ T_{0}<T,\\ &-\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2}(\lambda-\pi^{2}/L^{2})^{2}\cdot\int_{\Omega}[e^{2}_{1}+\frac{\alpha^{2}}{4}\gamma_{3}e^{4}_{1}]dx+o(|\lambda-\pi^{2}/L^{2}|^{2})&&\text{if}\ T>T_{0}.\end{aligned}\right.

Thus, the heat capacity CC at T=T0T=T_{0} satisfies

C+−C−=−T0​∂2F⁡(uT)∂T2|T0++T0​∂2F⁡(uT)∂T2|T0−=α1​T0​(d​λd​T)2|T=T0.C^{+}-C^{-}=-T_{0}\frac{\partial^{2}F(u^{T})}{\partial T^{2}}\Big|_{T_{0}^{+}}+T_{0}\frac{\partial^{2}F(u^{T})}{\partial T^{2}}\Big|_{T_{0}^{-}}=\alpha_{1}T_{0}\left(\frac{d\lambda}{dT}\right)^{2}|_{T=T_{0}}.

It is known that d​λ/d​T≠0d\lambda/dT\neq 0; hence the heat capacity at T=T0T=T_{0} has a finite jump.

From (3.14) we know that for the Type-III case, the critical exponent β=1\beta=1. Thus, it is not hard to deduce that the continuous phase transition in Type-III is of the 3rd order.

Appendix A Dynamic Transition Theory for Nonlinear Systems

In this appendix we recall some basic elements of the dynamic transition theory developed by the authors [3, 4], which are used to carry out the dynamic transition analysis for the binary systems in this article.

A.1. New classification scheme

Let XX and X1X_{1} be two Banach spaces, and X1⊂XX_{1}\subset X a compact and dense inclusion. In this chapter, we always consider the following nonlinear evolution equations

(A.1) d​ud​t=Lλ​u+G⁡(u,λ),u⁡(0)=φ,\left.\begin{aligned} &\frac{du}{dt}=L_{\lambda}u+G(u,\lambda),\\ &u(0)=\varphi,\end{aligned}\right.

where u:[0,∞)→Xu:[0,\infty)\rightarrow X is unknown function, and λ∈ℝ1\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{1} is the system parameter.

Assume that Lλ:X1→XL_{\lambda}:X_{1}\rightarrow X is a parameterized linear completely continuous field depending continuously on λ∈ℝ1\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{1}, which satisfies

(A.2) Lλ=−A+Bλa sectorial operator,A:X1→Xa linear homeomorphism,Bλ:X1→Xa linear compact operator.\left.\begin{aligned} &L_{\lambda}=-A+B_{\lambda}&&\text{a sectorial operator},\\ &A:X_{1}\rightarrow X&&\text{a linear homeomorphism},\\ &B_{\lambda}:X_{1}\rightarrow X&&\text{a linear compact operator}.\end{aligned}\right.

In this case, we can define the fractional order spaces XσX_{\sigma} for σ∈ℝ1\sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{1}. Then we also assume that G⁡(⋅,λ):Xα→XG(\cdot,\lambda):X_{\alpha}\rightarrow X is Cr​(r≥1)C^{r}(r\geq 1) bounded mapping for some 0≤α<10\leq\alpha<1, depending continuously on λ∈ℝ1\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{1}, and

(A.3) G⁡(u,λ)=o⁡(‖u‖Xα),∀λ∈ℝ1.G(u,\lambda)=o(\|u\|_{X_{\alpha}}),\ \ \ \ \forall\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{1}.

Hereafter we always assume the conditions (A.2) and (A.3), which represent that the system (A.1) has a dissipative structure.

Definition A.1.

We say that the system (A.1) has a transition of equilibrium from (u,λ)=(0,λ0)(u,\lambda)=(0,\lambda_{0}) on λ>λ0\lambda>\lambda_{0} (or 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁λ<λ0)\lambda<\lambda_{0}) if the following two conditions are satisfied:

  • (1)

    when λ<λ0\lambda<\lambda_{0} (or OPENλ>λ0),u=0\lambda>\lambda_{0}),u=0 is locally asymptotically stable for (A.1); and

  • (2)

    when λ>λ0\lambda>\lambda_{0} (or OPENλ<λ0)\lambda<\lambda_{0}), there exists a neighborhood U⊂XU\subset X of u=0u=0 independent of λ\lambda, such that for any φ∈U∖Γλ\varphi\in U\setminus\Gamma_{\lambda} the solution uλ​(t,φ)u_{\lambda}(t,\varphi) of (A.1) satisfies that

    lim supt→∞‖uλ​(t,φ)‖X≥δ⁡(λ)>0,limλ→λ0δ⁡(λ)≥0,\left.\begin{aligned} &\limsup_{t\rightarrow\infty}\|u_{\lambda}(t,\varphi)\|_{X}\geq\delta(\lambda)>0,\\ &\lim_{\lambda\rightarrow\lambda_{0}}\delta(\lambda)\geq 0,\end{aligned}\right.

    where Γλ\Gamma_{\lambda} is the stable manifold of u=0u=0, with codim Γλ≥1\Gamma_{\lambda}\geq 1 in XX for λ>λ0\lambda>\lambda_{0} (or OPENλ<λ0)\lambda<\lambda_{0}).

Obviously, the attractor bifurcation of (A.1) is a type of transition. However, bifurcation and transition are two different, but related concepts. Definition A.1 defines the transition of (A.1) from a stable equilibrium point to other states (not necessary equilibrium state). In general, we can define transitions from one attractor to another as follows.

Let the eigenvalues (counting multiplicity) of LλL_{\lambda} be given by

{βj(λ)∈ℂ|j=1,2,⋯}\{\beta_{j}(\lambda)\in\mathbb{C}\ \ |\ \ j=1,2,\cdots\}

Assume that

(A.4) Reβi(λ){<0 if ​λ<λ0,=0 if ​λ=λ0,>0 if ​λ>λ0,\displaystyle\text{Re}\ \beta_{i}(\lambda)\left\{\begin{aligned} &<0&&\text{ if }\lambda<\lambda_{0},\\ &=0&&\text{ if }\lambda=\lambda_{0},\\ &>0&&\text{ if }\lambda>\lambda_{0},\end{aligned}\right. ∀1≤i≤m,\displaystyle\forall 1\leq i\leq m,
(A.5) Re​βj​(λ0)<0\displaystyle\text{Re}\ \beta_{j}(\lambda_{0})<0 ∀j≥m+1.\displaystyle\forall j\geq m+1.

The following theorem is a basic principle of transitions from equilibrium states, which provides sufficient conditions and a basic classification for transitions of nonlinear dissipative systems. This theorem is a direct consequence of the center manifold theorems and the stable manifold theorems; we omit the proof.

Theorem A.1.

Let the conditions (A.4) and (A.5) hold true. Then, the system (A.1) must have a transition from (u,λ)=(0,λ0)(u,\lambda)=(0,\lambda_{0}), and there is a neighborhood U⊂XU\subset X of u=0u=0 such that the transition is one of the following three types:

  • (1)

    Continuous Transition: there exists an open and dense set U~λ⊂U\widetilde{U}_{\lambda}\subset U such that for any φ∈U~λ\varphi\in\widetilde{U}_{\lambda}, the solution uλ​(t,φ)u_{\lambda}(t,\varphi) of (A.1) satisfies

    limλ→λ0lim supt→∞‖uλ​(t,φ)‖X=0.\lim\limits_{\lambda\rightarrow\lambda_{0}}\limsup_{t\rightarrow\infty}\|u_{\lambda}(t,\varphi)\|_{X}=0.

    In particular, the attractor bifurcation of (A.1) at (0,λ0)(0,\lambda_{0}) is a continuous transition.

  • (2)

    Jump Transition: for any λ0<λ<λ0+ε\lambda_{0}<\lambda<\lambda_{0}+\varepsilon with some ε>0\varepsilon>0, there is an open and dense set Uλ⊂UU_{\lambda}\subset U such that for any φ∈Uλ\varphi\in U_{\lambda},

    lim supt→∞‖uλ​(t,φ)‖X≥δ>0,\limsup_{t\rightarrow\infty}\|u_{\lambda}(t,\varphi)\|_{X}\geq\delta>0,

    where δ>0\delta>0 is independent of λ\lambda. This type of transition is also called the discontinuous transition.

  • (3)

    Mixed Transition: for any λ0<λ<λ0+ε\lambda_{0}<\lambda<\lambda_{0}+\varepsilon with some ε>0\varepsilon>0, UU can be decomposed into two open sets U1λU^{\lambda}_{1} and U2λU^{\lambda}_{2} (UiλU^{\lambda}_{i} not necessarily connected):

    U¯=U¯1λ+U¯2λ,U1λ∩U2λ=∅,\bar{U}=\bar{U}^{\lambda}_{1}+\bar{U}^{\lambda}_{2},\ \ \ \ U^{\lambda}_{1}\cap U^{\lambda}_{2}=\emptyset,

    such that

    limλ→λ0lim supt→∞‖u⁡(t,φ)‖X=0\displaystyle\lim\limits_{\lambda\rightarrow\lambda_{0}}\limsup_{t\rightarrow\infty}\|u(t,\varphi)\|_{X}=0 ∀φ∈U1λ,\displaystyle\forall\varphi\in U^{\lambda}_{1},
    lim supt→∞‖u⁡(t,φ)‖X≥δ>0\displaystyle\limsup_{t\rightarrow\infty}\|u(t,\varphi)\|_{X}\geq\delta>0 ∀φ∈U2λ.\displaystyle\forall\varphi\in U^{\lambda}_{2}.

With this theorem in our disposal, we are in position to give a new dynamic classification scheme for dynamic phase transitions.

Definition A.1 (Dynamic Classification of Phase Transition).

The phase transitions for (A.1) at λ=λ0\lambda=\lambda_{0} is classified using their dynamic properties: continuous, jump, and mixed as given in Theorem A.1, which are called Type-I, Type-II and Type-III respectively.

An important aspect of the transition theory is to determine which of the three types of transitions given by Theorem A.1 occurs in a specific problem. By reduction to the center manifold of (A.1), we know that the type of transitions for (A.1) at (0,λ0)(0,\lambda_{0}) is completely dictated by its reduction equation near λ=λ0\lambda=\lambda_{0}, which can be expressed as:

(A.6) d​xd​t=Jλ​x+P​G​(x+Φ⁡(x,λ),λ) for ​x∈ℝm,\frac{dx}{dt}=J_{\lambda}x+PG(x+\Phi(x,\lambda),\lambda)\ \ \ \ \text{ for }x\in\mathbb{R}^{m},

where JλJ_{\lambda} is the m×mm\times m order Jordan matrix corresponding to the eigenvalues given by (A.4), Φ⁡(x,λ)\Phi(x,\lambda) is the center manifold function of (A.1) near λ0\lambda_{0}, P:X→EλP:X\rightarrow E_{\lambda} is the canonical projection, and

Eλ=∪1≤i≤m∪k∈N{u∈X1|(Lλ−βi(λ))ku=0}E_{\lambda}=\cup_{1\leq i\leq m}\cup_{k\in N}\{u\in X_{1}|\ \ (L_{\lambda}-\beta_{i}(\lambda))^{k}u=0\}

is the eigenspace of LλL_{\lambda}.

By the spectral theorem, (A.6) can be expressed into the following explicit form

(A.7) d​xd​t=Jλ​x+g⁡(x,λ),\frac{dx}{dt}=J_{\lambda}x+g(x,\lambda),

where

(A.8) g⁡(x,λ)=(g1​(x,λ),⋯,gm​(x,λ)),gj​(x,λ)=<G⁡(∑i=1mxi​ei+Φ⁡(x,λ),λ),ej∗>∀1≤j≤m.\left.\begin{aligned} &g(x,\lambda)=(g_{1}(x,\lambda),\cdots,g_{m}(x,\lambda)),\\ &g_{j}(x,\lambda)=<G(\sum^{m}_{i=1}x_{i}e_{i}+\Phi(x,\lambda),\lambda),e^{*}_{j}>\quad\forall 1\leq j\leq m.\end{aligned}\right.

Here eje_{j} and ej∗e^{*}_{j} (1≤j≤m)(1\leq j\leq m) are the eigenvectors of LλL_{\lambda} and Lλ∗L^{*}_{\lambda} respectively corresponding to the eigenvalues βj​(λ)\beta_{j}(\lambda) as in (A.4).

In particular, if G⁡(u,λ)G(u,\lambda) has the Taylor expansion

(A.9) G⁡(u,λ)=Gk​(u,λ)+o⁡(‖u‖Xαk),G(u,\lambda)=G_{k}(u,\lambda)+o(\|u\|^{k}_{X_{\alpha}}),

for some k≥2k\geq 2, where Gk​(u,λ)G_{k}(u,\lambda) is a kk-multilinear operator, then (A.7) can be rewritten as

(A.10) d​xd​t=Jλ​x+gk​(x,λ)+o⁡(|x|k),\frac{dx}{dt}=J_{\lambda}x+g_{k}(x,\lambda)+o(|x|^{k}),

where

gk​(x,λ)=(gk​1​(x,λ),⋯,gk​m​(x,λ)),\displaystyle g_{k}(x,\lambda)=(g_{k1}(x,\lambda),\cdots,g_{km}(x,\lambda)),
gk​j​(x,λ)=<Gk​(∑i=1nxi​ei,λ),ej∗>\displaystyle g_{kj}(x,\lambda)=<G_{k}(\sum^{n}_{i=1}x_{i}e_{i},\lambda),e^{*}_{j}> ∀1≤j≤m.\displaystyle\forall 1\leq j\leq m.

When x=0x=0 is an isolated singular point of gk​(x,λ)g_{k}(x,\lambda), in general the transition of (A.1) is determined by the first-order approximate bifurcation equation of (A.10) as follows:

(A.11) d​xd​t=Jλ​x+gk​(x,λ).\frac{dx}{dt}=J_{\lambda}x+g_{k}(x,\lambda).

The following theorem is useful to distinguish the transition types of (A.1) at (u,λ)=(0,λ0)(u,\lambda)=(0,\lambda_{0}).

Theorem A.2.

Let the conditions (A.4) and (A.5) hold true, and U⊂ℝmU\subset\mathbb{R}^{m} be a neighborhood of x=0x=0. Then we have the following assertions:

  • (1)

    If the transition of (A.1) at (0,λ0)(0,\lambda_{0}) is continuous, then there is an open and dense set U~⊂U\widetilde{U}\subset U such that for any x0∈U~x_{0}\in\widetilde{U} the solution x⁡(t,x0)x(t,x_{0}) of (A.7) at λ=λ0\lambda=\lambda_{0} with x⁡(0,x0)=x0x(0,x_{0})=x_{0} satisfies that

    limt→∞x⁡(t,x0)=0.\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}x(t,x_{0})=0.
  • (2)

    If there exists an open and dense set U~⊂U\widetilde{U}\subset U such that for any x0∈U~x_{0}\in\widetilde{U} the solution x⁡(t,x0)x(t,x_{0}) of (A.7) at λ=λ0\lambda=\lambda_{0} satisfies

    lim supt→∞|x⁡(t,x0)|≠0,\limsup_{t\rightarrow\infty}|x(t,x_{0})|\neq 0,

    then the transition is a jump transition.

  • (3)

    If the transition is mixed, then there exists an open set U~⊂U\widetilde{U}\subset U such that for any x0∈U~x_{0}\in\widetilde{U} the solution x⁡(t,x0)x(t,x_{0}) of (A.7) at λ=λ0\lambda=\lambda_{0} with x⁡(0,x0)=x0x(0,x_{0})=x_{0} satisfies

    limt→∞x⁡(t,x0)=0.\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}x(t,x_{0})=0.
  • (4)

    If the vector field in (A.7) at λ=λ0\lambda=\lambda_{0} satisfies

    <Jλ0x+g(x,λ0),x><0∀x∈U,x≠0,<J_{\lambda_{0}}x+g(x,\lambda_{0}),x><0\quad\forall x\in U,\ x\neq 0,

    then the transition of (A.1) at (0,λ0)(0,\lambda_{0}) is an Sm−1S^{m-1}-attractor bifurcation, and the transition is continuous.

  • (5)

    If the vector field g⁡(x,λ0)g(x,\lambda_{0}) given by (A.8) satisfies

    <g⁡(x,λ0),x>>0∀x∈U,x≠0,<g(x,\lambda_{0}),x>>0\ \ \ \ \forall x\in U,\ \ \ \ x\neq 0,

    then the transition is jump.

In general, the conditions in Assertions (1)-(3) of Theorem A.2 are not sufficient. They, however, do give sufficient conditions when (A.1) has a variational structure. To see this, let (A.1) be a gradient-type equation. Under the conditions (A.4) and (A.5), in a neighborhood U⊂XU\subset X of u=0u=0, the center manifold McM^{c} in UU at λ=λ0\lambda=\lambda_{0} consists three subsets

Mc=Wu+Ws+D,M^{c}=W^{u}+W^{s}+D,

where WsW^{s} is the stable set, WuW^{u} is the unstable set, and DD is the hyperbolic set of (A.7). Then we have the following theorem.

Theorem A.3.

Let (A.1) be a gradient-type equation, and the conditions (A.4) and (A.5) hold true. If u=0u=0 is an isolated singular point of (A.1) at λ=λ0\lambda=\lambda_{0}, then we have the following assertions:

  • (1)

    The transition of (A.1) at (u,λ)=(0,λ0)(u,\lambda)=(0,\lambda_{0}) is continuous if and only if u=0u=0 is locally asymptotically stable at λ=λ0\lambda=\lambda_{0}, i.e., the center manifold is stable: Mc=WsM^{c}=W^{s}. Moreover, (A.1) bifurcates from (0,λ0)(0,\lambda_{0}) to minimal attractors consisting of singular points of (A.1).

  • (2)

    If the stable set WsW^{s} of (A.1) has no interior points in McM^{c}, i.e., Mc=W¯u+D¯M^{c}=\bar{W}^{u}+\bar{D}, then the transition is jump.

A.2. Transitions from simple eigenvalues

We consider the transition of (A.1) from a simple critical eigenvalue. Let the eigenvalues βj​(λ)\beta_{j}(\lambda) of LλL_{\lambda} satisfy (A.4) and (A.5) with m=1m=1. Then the first eigenvalue β1​(λ)\beta_{1}(\lambda) must be a real eigenvalue. Let e1​(λ)e_{1}(\lambda) and e1∗​(λ)e^{*}_{1}(\lambda) be the eigenvectors of LλL_{\lambda} and Lλ∗L^{*}_{\lambda} respectively corresponding to β1​(λ)\beta_{1}(\lambda) with

Lλ0​e1=0,Lλ0∗​e1∗=0,<e1,e1∗>=1.L_{\lambda_{0}}e_{1}=0,\ \ \ \ L^{*}_{\lambda_{0}}e^{*}_{1}=0,\ \ \ \ <e_{1},e^{*}_{1}>=1.

Let Φ⁡(x,λ)\Phi(x,\lambda) be the center manifold function of (A.1) near λ=λ0\lambda=\lambda_{0}. We assume that

(A.12) <G⁡(x​e1+Φ⁡(x,λ0),λ0),e1∗>=α​xk+o⁡(|x|k),<G(xe_{1}+\Phi(x,\lambda_{0}),\lambda_{0}),e^{*}_{1}>=\alpha x^{k}+o(|x|^{k}),

Theorem A.4.

Assume (A.4) and (A.5) with m=1m=1, and (A.12). If kk=odd and α≠0\alpha\neq 0 in (A.12) then the following assertions hold true:

    v1,2λ=±|β1​(λ)/α|1/k−1​e1​(λ)+o⁡(|β1|1/k−1).v^{\lambda}_{1,2}=\pm|\beta_{1}(\lambda)/\alpha|^{{1}/{k-1}}e_{1}(\lambda)+o(|\beta_{1}|^{{1}/{k-1}}).

Assume (A.4) and (A.5) with m=1m=1, and (A.12). If kk=even and α≠0\alpha\neq 0, then we have the following assertions:

More precisely, there exists a neighborhood U⊂XU\subset X of u=0u=0 such that UU is separated into two disjoint open sets U1λU^{\lambda}_{1} and U2λU^{\lambda}_{2} by the stable manifold Γλ\Gamma_{\lambda} of u=0u=0 satisfying the following properties:

    limt→∞‖u⁡(t,φ)−vλ‖X=0,\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}\|u(t,\varphi)-v^{\lambda}\|_{X}=0,

A.3. Singular Separation

In this section, we study an important problem associated with the discontinuous transition of (A.1), which we call the singular separation.

Definition A.2.
  1. (1)

    An invariant set Σ\Sigma of (A.1) is called a singular element if Σ\Sigma is either a singular point or a periodic orbit.

  2. (2)

    Let Σ1⊂X\Sigma_{1}\subset X be a singular element of (A.1) and U⊂XU\subset X a neighborhood of Σ1\Sigma_{1}. We say that (A.1) has a singular separation of Σ\Sigma at λ=λ1\lambda=\lambda_{1} if

    1. (a)

      (A.1) has no singular elements in UU as λ<λ1\lambda<\lambda_{1} (or λ>λ1\lambda>\lambda_{1}), and generates a singular element Σ1⊂U\Sigma_{1}\subset U at λ=λ1\lambda=\lambda_{1}, and

    2. (b)

      there are branches of singular elements Σλ\Sigma_{\lambda}, which are separated from Σ1\Sigma_{1} for λ>λ1\lambda>\lambda_{1} (or λ<λ1\lambda<\lambda_{1}), i.e.,

      limλ→λ1maxx∈Σλ⁡dist​(x,Σ1)=0.\lim\limits_{\lambda\rightarrow\lambda_{1}}\max_{x\in\Sigma_{\lambda}}\text{dist}(x,\Sigma_{1})=0.

A special case of singular separation is the saddle-node bifurcation defined as follows.

Definition A.3.

Let u1∈Xu_{1}\in X be a singular point of (A.1) at λ=λ1\lambda=\lambda_{1} with u1≠0u_{1}\neq 0. We say that (A.1) has a saddle-node bifurcation at (u1,λ1)(u_{1},\lambda_{1}) if

  1. (1)

    the index of Lλ+GL_{\lambda}+G at (u1,λ1)(u_{1},\lambda_{1}) is zero, i.e., ind(−(Lλ1+G),u1)=0(-(L_{\lambda_{1}}+G),u_{1})=0,

  2. (2)

    there are two branches Γ1​(λ)\Gamma_{1}(\lambda) and Γ2​(λ)\Gamma_{2}(\lambda) of singular points of (A.1), which are separated from u1u_{1} for λ>λ1\lambda>\lambda_{1} (or OPENλ<λ1)\lambda<\lambda_{1}), i.e., for any uλ∈Γi​(λ)u_{\lambda}\in\Gamma_{i}(\lambda) (i=1,2)(i=1,2) we have

    uλ→u1​in​Xas​λ→λ1,u_{\lambda}\rightarrow u_{1}\ \text{in}\ X\ \ \ \ \text{as}\ \lambda\rightarrow\lambda_{1},

    and

  3. (3)

    the indices of uλi∈Γi​(λ)u^{i}_{\lambda}\in\Gamma_{i}(\lambda) are as follows

    ind(−(Lλ+G),uλ)={1 if ​uλ∈Γ2​(λ),−1 if ​uλ∈Γ1​(λ).\text{ind}(-(L_{\lambda}+G),u_{\lambda})=\left\{\begin{aligned} &1&&\text{ if }u_{\lambda}\in\Gamma_{2}(\lambda),\\ &-1&&\text{ if }u_{\lambda}\in\Gamma_{1}(\lambda).\end{aligned}\right.

Intuitively, the saddle-node bifurcation is schematically shown as in Figure A.4, where the singular points in Γ1​(λ)\Gamma_{1}(\lambda) are saddle points and in Γ2​(λ)\Gamma_{2}(\lambda) are nodes, and the singular separation of periodic orbits is as in shown Figure A.5.

For the singular separation we can give a general principle as follows, which provides a basis for singular separation theory.

Theorem A.6.

Let the conditions (A.4) and (A.5) hold true. Then we have the following assertions.

Appendix B Ginzburg-Landau Models

In this subsection, we introduce the time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau model for equilibrium phase transitions.

We start with thermodynamic potentials and the Ginzburg-Landau free energy. As we know, four thermodynamic potentials– internal energy, the enthalpy, the Helmholtz free energy and the Gibbs free energy–are useful in the chemical thermodynamics of reactions and non-cyclic processes.

Consider a thermal system, its order parameter uu changes in Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} (1≤n≤3)(1\leq n\leq 3). In this situation, the free energy of this system is of the form

(B.1) ℋ⁡(u,λ)=ℋ0+∫Ω[12​∑i=1mμi​|∇ui|2+g⁡(u,∇u,λ)]​𝑑x{\mathcal{H}}(u,\lambda)={\mathcal{H}}_{0}+\int_{\Omega}\Big[\frac{1}{2}\sum^{m}_{i=1}\mu_{i}|\nabla u_{i}|^{2}+g(u,\nabla u,\lambda)\Big]dx

where N≥3N\geq 3 is an integer, u=(u1,⋯,um),μi=μi​(λ)>0u=(u_{1},\cdots,u_{m}),\mu_{i}=\mu_{i}(\lambda)>0, and g⁡(u,∇u,λ)g(u,\nabla u,\lambda) is a Cr​(r≥2)C^{r}(r\geq 2) function of (u,∇u)(u,\nabla u) with the Taylor expansion

(B.2) g⁡(u,∇u,λ)=∑αi​j​k​ui​Dj​uk+∑|I|=1NαI​uI+o⁡(|u|N)−f​X,g(u,\nabla u,\lambda)=\sum\alpha_{ijk}u_{i}D_{j}u_{k}+\sum^{N}_{|I|=1}\alpha_{I}u^{I}+o(|u|^{N})-fX,

where I=(i1,⋯,im),ik≥0I=(i_{1},\cdots,i_{m}),i_{k}\geq 0 are integer, |I|=∑k=1mik|I|=\sum^{m}_{k=1}i_{k}, the coefficients αi​j​k\alpha_{ijk} and αI\alpha_{I} continuously depend on λ\lambda, which are determined by the concrete physical problem, uI=ui11⋯ui​mmu^{I}=u^{i_{1}}_{1}\cdots u^{im}_{m} and f​XfX the generalized work.

A thermal system is controlled by some parameter λ\lambda. When λ\lambda is far from the critical point λ0\lambda_{0} the system lies on a stable equilibrium state Σ1\Sigma_{1}, and when λ\lambda reaches or exceeds λ0\lambda_{0} the state Σ1\Sigma_{1} becomes unstable, and meanwhile the system will undergo a transition from Σ1\Sigma_{1} to another stable state Σ2\Sigma_{2}. The basic principle is that there often exists fluctuations in the system leading to a deviation from the equilibrium states, and the phase transition process is a dynamical behavior, which should be described by a time-dependent equation.

To derive a general time-dependent model, first we recall that the classical le Châtelier principle amounts to saying that for a stable equilibrium state of a system Σ\Sigma, when the system deviates from Σ\Sigma by a small perturbation or fluctuation, there will be a resuming force to restore this system to return to the stable state Σ\Sigma. Second, we know that a stable equilibrium state of a thermal system must be the minimal value point of the thermodynamic potential.

By the mathematical characterization of gradient systems and the le Châtelier principle, for a system with thermodynamic potential ℋ⁡(u,λ){\mathcal{H}}(u,\lambda), the governing equations are essentially determined by the functional ℋ⁡(u,λ){\mathcal{H}}(u,\lambda). When the order parameters (u1,⋯,um)(u_{1},\cdots,u_{m}) are nonconserved variables, i.e., the integers

∫Ωui​(x,t)​𝑑x=ai​(t)≠constant.\int_{\Omega}u_{i}(x,t)dx=a_{i}(t)\neq\text{constant}.

then the time-dependent equations are given by

(B.3) ∂ui∂t=−βi​δδ​ui​ℋ​(u,λ)+Φi​(u,∇u,λ),∂u∂n|∂Ω=0(or​u|∂Ω=0),u⁡(x,0)=φ⁡(x),\left.\begin{aligned} &\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial t}=-\beta_{i}\frac{\delta}{\delta u_{i}}{\mathcal{H}}(u,\lambda)+\Phi_{i}(u,\nabla u,\lambda),\\ &\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}|_{\partial\Omega}=0\ \ \ \ (\text{or}\ u|_{\partial\Omega}=0),\\ &u(x,0)=\varphi(x),\end{aligned}\right.

for any 1≤i≤m1\leq i\leq m, where δ/δ​ui\delta/\delta u_{i} are the variational derivative, βi>0\beta_{i}>0 and Φi\Phi_{i} satisfy

(B.4) ∫Ω∑iΦi​δδ​ui​ℋ​(u,λ)​𝑑x=0.\int_{\Omega}\sum_{i}\Phi_{i}\frac{\delta}{\delta u_{i}}{\mathcal{H}}(u,\lambda)dx=0.

The condition (B.4) is required by the Le Châtelier principle. In the concrete problem, the terms Φi\Phi_{i} can be determined by physical laws and (B.4).

When the order parameters are the number density and the system has no material exchange with the external, then uju_{j} (1≤j≤m)(1\leq j\leq m) are conserved, i.e.,

(B.5) ∫Ωuj​(x,t)​𝑑x=constant.\int_{\Omega}u_{j}(x,t)dx=\text{constant}.

This conservation law requires a continuous equation

(B.6) ∂uj∂t=−∇⋅Jj(u,λ),\frac{\partial u_{j}}{\partial t}=-\nabla\cdot J_{j}(u,\lambda),

where Jj​(u,λ)J_{j}(u,\lambda) is the flux of component uju_{j}. In addition, JjJ_{j} satisfy

(B.7) Jj=−kj∇(μj−∑i≠jμi),J_{j}=-k_{j}\nabla(\mu_{j}-\sum_{i\neq j}\mu_{i}),

where μl\mu_{l} is the chemical potential of component ulu_{l},

(B.8) μj−∑i≠jμi=δδ​uj​ℋ​(u,λ)−ϕj​(u,∇u,λ),\mu_{j}-\sum_{i\neq j}\mu_{i}=\frac{\delta}{\delta u_{j}}{\mathcal{H}}(u,\lambda)-\phi_{j}(u,\nabla u,\lambda),

and ϕj​(u,λ)\phi_{j}(u,\lambda) is a function depending on the other components uiu_{i} (i≠j)(i\neq j). When m=1m=1, i.e., the system consists of two components AA and BB, this term ϕj=0\phi_{j}=0. Thus, from (B.6)-(B.8) we obtain the dynamical equations as follows

(B.9) ∂uj∂t=βj​Δ​[δδ​uj​ℋ​(u,λ)−ϕj​(u,∇u,λ)],∂u∂n|∂Ω=0,∂Δ​u∂n|∂Ω=0,u⁡(x,0)=φ⁡(x),\left.\begin{aligned} &\frac{\partial u_{j}}{\partial t}=\beta_{j}\Delta\left[\frac{\delta}{\delta u_{j}}{\mathcal{H}}(u,\lambda)-\phi_{j}(u,\nabla u,\lambda)\right],\\ &\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}|_{\partial\Omega}=0,\ \ \ \ \frac{\partial\Delta u}{\partial n}|_{\partial\Omega}=0,\\ &u(x,0)=\varphi(x),\end{aligned}\right.

for 1≤j≤m1\leq j\leq m, where βj>0\beta_{j}>0 are constants, ϕj\phi_{j} satisfy

(B.10) ∫Ω∑jΔ​ϕj⋅δδ​uj​ℋ​(u,λ)​𝑑x=0.\int_{\Omega}\sum_{j}\Delta\phi_{j}\cdot\frac{\delta}{\delta u_{j}}{\mathcal{H}}(u,\lambda)dx=0.

If the order parameters (u1,⋯,uk)(u_{1},\cdots,u_{k}) are coupled to the conserved variables (uk+1,⋯,um)(u_{k+1},\cdots,u_{m}), then the dynamical equations are

(B.11) ∂ui∂t=−βi​δδ​ui​ℋ​(u,λ)+Φi​(u,∇u,λ),∂uj∂t=βj​Δ​[δδ​uj​ℋ​(u,λ)−ϕj​(u,∇u,λ)],∂ui∂n|∂Ω=0(or​ui|∂Ω=0),∂uj∂n|∂Ω=0,∂Δ​uj∂n|∂Ω=0,u⁡(x,0)=φ⁡(x).\left.\begin{aligned} &\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial t}=-\beta_{i}\frac{\delta}{\delta u_{i}}{\mathcal{H}}(u,\lambda)+\Phi_{i}(u,\nabla u,\lambda),\\ &\frac{\partial u_{j}}{\partial t}=\beta_{j}\Delta\left[\frac{\delta}{\delta u_{j}}{\mathcal{H}}(u,\lambda)-\phi_{j}(u,\nabla u,\lambda)\right],\\ &\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial n}|_{\partial\Omega}=0\ \ \ \ (\text{or}\ u_{i}|_{\partial\Omega}=0),\\ &\frac{\partial u_{j}}{\partial n}|_{\partial\Omega}=0,\ \ \ \ \frac{\partial\Delta u_{j}}{\partial n}|_{\partial\Omega}=0,\\ &u(x,0)=\varphi(x).\end{aligned}\right.

for 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k and k+1≤j≤mk+1\leq j\leq m.

The model (B.11) gives a general form of the governing equations to thermodynamic phase transitions. Hence, the dynamics of equilibrium phase transition in statistic physics is based on the new Ginzburg-Landau formulation (B.11).

Physically, the initial value condition u⁡(0)=φu(0)=\varphi in (B.11) stands for the fluctuation of system or perturbation from the external. Hence, φ\varphi is generally small. However, we can not exclude the possibility of a bigger noise φ\varphi.
